claims.claim: Roger Tichborne, the heir, vanished at age 25
claims.quote: Roger Tichborne, heir to the family's title and fortunes, was presumed to have died in a shipwreck in 1854 at age 25.

claims.claim: His mother recognised/accepted a butcher as her son
claims.quote: In 1866, a Wagga Wagga butcher known as Thomas Castro came forward claiming to be Roger Tichborne. ... He was instantly accepted by Lady Tichborne as her son

claims.claim: Roger Tichborne sailed from Rio in 1854
claims.quote: The last positive sightings of Roger were in Rio de Janeiro, in April 1854, awaiting a sea passage to Jamaica. Although he lacked a passport he secured a berth on a ship, the Bella, which sailed for Jamaica on 20 April.

claims.claim: The Bella's capsized boat was found four days after she sailed
claims.quote: On 24 April 1854 a capsized ship's boat bearing the name Bella was discovered off the Brazilian coast, together with some wreckage but no personnel, and the ship's loss with all hands was assumed.

claims.claim: No survivors of the Bella
claims.quote: together with some wreckage but no personnel, and the ship's loss with all hands was assumed

claims.claim: The portrait of Roger is a daguerreotype by Thomas Helsby taken in Santiago in 1853, public domain
claims.quote: Description: A daguerreotype of Roger Charles Doughty Tichborne, taken in Santiago, Chile Date: 1853 Author: Thomas Helsby

claims.claim: By 1867 the Claimant weighed nearly 300 pounds
claims.quote: By mid-June 1867 the Claimant's weight had reached almost 300 pounds (21 st; 140 kg) and would increase even more in the ensuing years.

claims.claim: Roger Tichborne was remembered as slender
claims.quote: whose 189-pound (13.5 st; 86 kg) weight contrasted sharply with Roger's remembered slender build

claims.claim: The Claimant gained 40 pounds on the voyage to England alone
claims.quote: Good living in Sydney had raised his weight on departure to 210 pounds (15 st; 95 kg), and during the long voyage he added another 40 pounds (2.9 st; 18 kg).

claims.claim: The four-portrait card is titled 'Four Portraits from Life of the Claimant' and dates from 1873
claims.quote: FOUR PORTRAITS FROM LIFE, OF THE CLAIMANT.

claims.claim: The bankrupt butcher's pipe was marked R.C.T.
claims.quote: During his bankruptcy examination Castro had mentioned an entitlement to property in England. He had also talked of experiencing a shipwreck and was smoking a briar pipe which carried the initials "R.C.T."

claims.claim: In Wagga Wagga he traded as Thomas Castro
claims.quote: T CASTRO BUTCHER.

claims.claim: Challenged by a lawyer, he agreed he was Roger Tichborne
claims.quote: William Gibbes, a lawyer from Wagga Wagga, had identified Roger Tichborne in the person of a bankrupt local butcher using the name Thomas Castro. ... When challenged by Gibbes to reveal his true name, Castro had initially been reticent but eventually agreed that he was indeed the missing Roger Tichborne

claims.claim: Two witnesses swore to the marks on Roger's arm and drew different marks
claims.quote: Fac-simile of drawing made by Lady Doughty, and sworn by her to be the marks she saw on Roger Tichborne's arm. ... As these marks, sworn to by the two persons so widely differ, there are only two possibilities.

claims.claim: Lord Bellew said Roger had tattoos the Claimant lacked
claims.quote: Lord Bellew, who had known Roger Tichborne at Stonyhurst, testified that Roger had distinctive body tattoos which the Claimant did not possess.

claims.claim: Soon after Bellew's testimony, the jury said it had heard enough
claims.quote: On 4 March the jury notified the judge that they had heard enough and were ready to reject the Claimant's suit.

claims.claim: The tattoo drawings come from 'The Tichborne Case in a Nutshell', 1874
claims.quote: Archive title: File:The Tichborne case in a nutshell, by A Lover of Truth, 1874

claims.claim: The criminal trial occupied 188 court days
claims.quote: The trial, one of the lengthiest cases heard in an English court, began on 21 April 1873 and lasted until 28 February 1874, occupying 188 court days.

claims.claim: 215 witnesses were called
claims.quote: Altogether, Hawkins called 215 witnesses, including numbers from France, Melipilla, Australia and Wapping

claims.claim: The jury returned its verdict within 30 minutes
claims.quote: The jury retired at noon on Saturday 28 February, and returned to the court within 30 minutes.

claims.claim: The Claimant was barred from testifying at the criminal trial
claims.quote: Under the legal rules that then applied to criminal cases, the Claimant, though present in court, was not allowed to testify.

claims.claim: Mark Twain saw him feted in London, and reported he was called 'Sir Roger' by everyone
claims.quote: the American writer Mark Twain, who was then in London, attended an event at which the Claimant was present and "thought him a rather fine and stately figure". Twain observed that the company were "educated men, men moving in good society. ... It was 'Sir Roger', always 'Sir Roger' on all hands, no one withheld the title".

claims.claim: The courtroom painting is by Frederick Sargent and depicts the Tichborne trial
claims.quote: Archive title: File:The Tichborne Trial by Frederick Sargent.jpg

claims.claim: The jury declared him to be Arthur Orton, a butcher's son from Wapping
claims.quote: Their verdict declared that the Claimant was not Roger Tichborne, that he had not seduced Katherine Doughty, and that he was indeed Arthur Orton.

claims.claim: Arthur Orton was a butcher's son from Wapping
claims.quote: Arthur Orton, a butcher's son from Wapping in London, who had gone to sea as a boy and had last been heard of in Australia

claims.claim: He served 10 years
claims.quote: The Claimant was released on licence on 11 October 1884 after serving 10 years.

claims.claim: He confessed for a fee in 1895, then retracted
claims.quote: In 1895, for a fee of a few hundred pounds, he confessed in The People newspaper that he was, after all, Arthur Orton. ... he quickly retracted the confession and insisted again that he was Roger Tichborne.

claims.claim: Woodruff argued in 1957 that doubt remains
claims.quote: Woodruff submits that the legal verdicts, although fair given the evidence before the courts, have not fully resolved the "great doubt" that Cockburn admitted hung over the case. Woodruff wrote in 1957

claims.claim: The Hyde Park meeting illustration is by F. T. Lix, published in Le Monde illustré in 1875
claims.quote: Archive title: File:Meeting pour Tichborne à Hyde Park (Monde illustré, 1875-04-10).jpeg ... Date: 1875 Author: Frédéric Théodore Lix

claims.claim: Roger Tichborne was heir to a Hampshire baronetcy
claims.quote: The Tichbornes, of Tichborne Park near Alresford in Hampshire, were an old English Catholic family

claims.claim: His mother refused to believe he was dead and advertised in Australian newspapers for news of him
claims.quote: His mother, Lady Tichborne, clung to a belief that he might have survived, and after hearing rumours that he had made his way to Australia, she advertised extensively in Australian newspapers, offering a reward for information.

claims.claim: Lady Tichborne accepted him the moment she saw his face in a Paris hotel
claims.quote: This meeting took place on 11 January at the Hôtel de Lille. As soon as she saw his face, Lady Tichborne accepted him.

claims.claim: She settled £1,000 a year on him
claims.quote: She settled an income of £1,000 a year on him

claims.claim: Almost no other member of the Tichborne family accepted him
claims.quote: Apart from Lady Tichborne, a distant cousin, Anthony John Wright Biddulph, was the only relation who accepted the Claimant as genuine

claims.claim: Roger grew up speaking French, and the Claimant spoke none
claims.quote: Lady Tichborne's brother Henry Seymour denounced the Claimant as false when he found that the latter neither spoke nor understood French (Roger's first language as a child) and lacked any trace of a French accent.

claims.claim: The Claimant had a pronounced cockney accent
claims.quote: journalists following the campaign often commented on his pronounced cockney accent, suggestive of East London origins

claims.claim: Australian station records held no Thomas Castro but did list an Arthur Orton
claims.quote: These showed no reference to "Thomas Castro", although the employment of an "Arthur Orton" was recorded.

claims.claim: The civil jury stopped the case in 1872
claims.quote: On 4 March the jury notified the judge that they had heard enough and were ready to reject the Claimant's suit.

claims.claim: He was sentenced to fourteen years
claims.quote: the Claimant was sentenced to two consecutive terms of seven years' imprisonment

claims.claim: Released in 1884, he toured music halls
claims.quote: instead signing a contract to tour with music halls and circuses

claims.claim: He died destitute in 1898
claims.quote: His shop failed, as did other business attempts, and he died destitute, of heart disease, on 1 April 1898.

claims.claim: About 5,000 people came to the pauper's grave
claims.quote: around 5,000 people attended Paddington Cemetery for the burial in an unmarked pauper's grave

claims.claim: The family allowed a card reading "Sir Roger Charles Doughty Tichborne" on the coffin
claims.quote: the Tichborne family allowed a card bearing the name "Sir Roger Charles Doughty Tichborne" to be placed on the coffin before its interment

claims.claim: Woodruff argued the imposture was too improbable to invent from scratch, and that the Claimant just conceivably was Roger
claims.quote: Woodruff's principal argument is the sheer improbability that anyone could conceive such an imposture from scratch, at such a distance, and then implement it
